Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh… –Matthew 19:6.

The marriage relationship was authored by God in the very beginning of time. God also offered to bless the marriage (Genesis 1:28) of the man and woman entering into it, if they desired to maintain its beauty and holiness. Since then, Satan has attempted, in every way possible, to corrupt and destroy the existence of Holy Matrimony. As early as Genesis 4:19, mankind was using polygamy to corrupt God's design of marriage. In Leviticus chapters 21 and 22, a plan, called a divorce, was put in place to legally dissolve the “first love”. This also included the option to remarry. When it was first developed as a practice, the call for divorce was initiated by man, not God, and was for the purpose of dissolving what was understood up until that time to be a lifelong commitment.

In this article we want to look at a number of points:

  • What does the Bible teach about marriage? Does the first marriage carry any special position with God?
  • What does the Bible teach about divorce? Does God recognize divorce as terminating the original marriage vow while either spouse is still living?
  • What does the Bible teach about the reuniting of a separated or divorced first marriage?

It is the desire of this study to be comprehensive, while allowing the scriptures to be their own interpreter, thus keeping commentary to a minimum. The purpose of this writing is to encourage diligence with prayer in seeking the will of God through a study of His Word. The desire of the writer has been to prayerfully consider all relevant scriptures and the context for which they were written.

What does the Bible teach about God's view of the first marriage?

At least five times in the Old Testament, the first marriage is described by the Lord as exclusive and lifelong. This same view was supported by Jesus and the apostles in the New Testament.

  1. Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth –Proverbs 5:18. Note the attention given to the wife of thy youth.

  2. For the LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God –Isaiah 54:6. Being a wife of one’s youth and then later refused, intensified the grieving of this forsaken woman.

  3. Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant. And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously. –Malachi 2:14-16. And why are they made one, exclusive to each other? To raise up a godly seed unto the Lord. Even though God hates putting away, men still try to cover it with a garment of civil, legal acceptance called "divorce".

  4. Matthew 19:3-12: V.4 In the beginning… Jesus, when asked by the Pharisees about this issue, takes them back to original intent of His Father when He chides them… And he answered and said unto them, Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female –Matthew 19:4. He then goes on to remind them of the Scriptures teaching that …a man [shall] leave [his] father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder –Matthew 19:5-6. Don't equate man’s authority (the civil court) with God’s authority when it comes to deciding what the facts are concerning marriage, divorce, and remarriage. We need to remember that it is God who has joined each marriage together in Heaven and has recorded them in the Book of Life.

  5. For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband. So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man –Romans 7:2-3. Again, this is pointing back to the beginning in order to establish a basis of Truth.

Only the death of either spouse will terminate the initial marriage covenant in the heavenly records. And once this life is over, only the heavenly records will matter—for all of eternity.

There are several exceptions to the Biblical ideal:

  • Defraud [deprive, keep back] ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency [lack of self-restraint] –1 Corinthians 7:5. So, restraining the marriage relationship for a time with voluntary consent from both husband and wife when there is a need for seeking God’s favor or guidance on a matter of great importance, may in some circumstances find God’s blessing. However, this should only be engaged in with a clear understanding and commitment by both spouses involved, about when and how to come together again, lest Satan tempt you. This exception has three clear qualifiers… 1) with consent, 2) for a time, & 3) for the purpose of giving yourselves to prayer and fasting.

  • And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband: But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife –1 Corinthians 7:10-11. This is the Scriptural passage that frees the innocent spouse from biblical guilt when the other spouse is the one who chose to part ways. However, the teaching still remains that they shall not marry another “so long as the original partner remains alive”.

What does the Bible teach about God's view of divorce?

It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery –Matthew 5:31-32. As Jesus taught the people in His Sermon on the Mount, one of the many things that He kept focusing on was this issue of God’s original plan for marriage.

“Saving for the cause of fornication” Fornication is any type of immorality prior to marriage. Modern-day Christianity, at times, struggles with this idea since the customs of the ancient Jewish culture have long since been forgotten. In Jewish culture, the betrothal period was considered almost as binding as the marriage ceremony itself, so much so that to end a betrothal required a “divorce”. With this as a foundational understanding, fornication here is speaking of immorality during the espousal or betrothal period. If any unfaithfulness was discovered, a writing of divorcement was required to break the betrothal, espousal, or engagement. This specific aspect of divorce was not criticized by Jesus. Even though they were not permitted to engage in the physical relationship of marriage during the betrothal period, they were still referred to as husband and wife. Finally, the reason this is referred to as fornication instead of adultery is because that during the betrothal period the marriage of the two has not yet taken place, nor has their relationship been consummated physically. Thus, just prior to the point in time when they are considered by God as being married, any outside relationship would be fornication, while just after they are considered married, any similar relationship would be adultery.

We have an excellent biblical example of this type of situation with Joseph & Mary in the following verses: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily –Matthew 1:18, 19.

So, biblically speaking, divorce can put asunder the first marriage according to civil law but cannot terminate a first marriage before God. A divorced person remains the companion of their first marriage (as long as the other spouse is alive) even when remarrying, whether they are legally divorced or not, thus resulting in biblical adultery for both parties. However, when divorce is allowed to be recognized as being legitimate in breaking or annulling the initial marriage covenant, we have thereby removed the specific reason by which God calls subsequent marriages adultery.

In Matthew 19:3-10, Jesus is teaching the same lesson as in Matthew 5:31-32. However, Matthew 19:3-10 was initiated from an attempt by the Pharisees to trap Jesus with a question: They say unto him, Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away? –Matthew 19:7. Jesus then responds further and says, …Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8.

Also, in Mark it is written, But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female. For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and cleave to his wife; And they twain shall be one flesh: so then they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder –Mark 10:6-9.

Thus, divorce, with all its regulations, is man's attempt to use civil law to terminate that which from the beginning was understood to be until the death of either spouse.

What does the Bible teach about the reuniting of a separated or a divorced first marriage?

He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8. Here Jesus is teaching the initial mind of His Father. In the law, Moses taught that… When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house. And when she is departed out of his house, she may go and be another man's wife. And if the latter husband hate her, and write her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand, and sendeth her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, which took her to be his wife; Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife… –Deuteronomy 24:1-4.

This is Moses' teaching regarding permission and qualifications for divorce which Jesus explained was because of the hardness of their hearts. Jesus further clarified this by saying, but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8.

Perhaps Jeremiah also is referring to Moses' writing in Deuteronomy 24:1-4 when he says, They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man's, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted? but thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the LORD –Jeremiah 3:1. The remainder of Jeremiah chapter 3 speaks of God receiving them back if they repent. God pleads for them to (v.13) "acknowledge thine iniquity" (repent), and repeatedly calls for their return (v.14-)

God invited Israel back into fellowship with Him on the basis of acknowledging her sin and changing her ways, giving no heed to the instruction that Moses gave in Deuteronomy 24:1-4, because "from the beginning it was not so."

In Jeremiah 3:8, the Lord had put her (Israel) away and given her a bill of divorcement. But in verses 1 and 12, He invites her to return and in verse 14 He offers the terms of reconciliation. In Malachi it is written, Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god –Malachi 2:11.

God's divorcing of Israel and Israel's subsequent remarriage to a strange god in no way interfered with them returning to their first marriage. Instead, the Lord invited them back if they would repent, Jeremiah 3:13-14. By the time of Deuteronomy chapter 24 and through most of the Old Testament, divorce was the accepted normal, with mankind attempting to put some regulations on it, "but from the beginning it was not so."

In the book of Hosea, we have a biblical example of the reuniting of a separated or divorced first marriage: … And the LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD –Hosea 1:2 (see also Hosea 2:5).

Sometime after Hosea marries her, she resorts to the life of a "harlot'' (Hosea 3:3) and goes after other "lovers" (2:7). When she refers to Hosea as "my first husband" (2:7), it is evidence that she likely remarried after deserting Hosea. (2:14) By Hosea patiently "alluring her and speaking comfortably to her" (2:19-20), Hosea betrothed her again and Gomer apparently responded (2:20) "in faithfulness” and came to "know the Lord." (3:3) Eventually, Hosea and Gomer both reunited with a commitment of faithfulness to each other.

Restoration to the initial God-ordained commitment is the goal, reconciliation is the process, and a repentant heart before the Lord for His mercy and forgiveness is the means (see Hosea 3:5).

John 4:1-42 is a scripture that some would interpret as objecting to the reuniting of a first marriage after a separation or divorce, because of Jesus' reply to the woman. After she said …I have no husband. Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly –John 4:17-18.

Some would interpret Jesus to be saying, "You are right woman, none of your five former husbands of which you have divorced or put away (including your first one) are your husband, and neither is the one you have now. Some commentators and others refer to this woman as a five-time divorcee and currently living with a man in an unmarried state. However, I find no evidence in this account that this woman was living an unholy life.

Jesus' purpose of this account is to reveal Himself as the "Messias" with "Living Water" to this woman and many more in Sychar. Jesus says nothing to fault or correct her, which He typically would when meeting with sin. All five husbands could have been passed away and the one she was now seeing, just a friend, perhaps anticipating marriage. Also, we don't know since it doesn't say, but she seemed to be a woman of respect and influence in the city, which would have been unlikely with an ongoing reputation of immorality. Jesus would surely have said something to inform her of her sin, when making available His Living Water. So, to use this account and say that all five husbands are adulterous and still classified as God-recorded husbands does not agree with the rest of Scripture. Nor does it support the context of the statement: he whom thou now hast is not thy husband. To claim that this story is a display of an immoral lifestyle with no known biblical evidence is close to “adding to” or “taking away” from the Scriptures. (See Revelation 22:18)

In conclusion… In our world today and in history past, mankind has attempted to equate subsequent marriages following a divorce, to the level of the initial marriage covenant. This has confused the emphasis and intent God has put on the initial marriage covenant. God's Word teaches that the Lord has always respected repentance in the restoration of any initial God-blessed covenant. For the Lord to bless and prosper the reconciling of any struggling relationship, He requires a broken, contrite spirit of humility and repentance with submission.

The context of 1 Corinthians 7:10-16 is that of a believer being in a covenant relationship with a spouse who is an unbeliever. In verse 15, the remaining believing spouse is not under obligation to denounce their walk of faith to continue a marriage relationship, neither are they free to remarry (verse 11) in the event of the unbelieving spouse leaving. If verse 15 is speaking of the marriage covenant, then verse 39 would contradict verse 15 and the will of God according to the rest of Scripture, (see Matthew 19:5 and 1 Corinthians 7:10). Living separately limits influence to the family and is a negative witness to the community, thus the believing spouse will always have a much greater impact for the Lord by staying true to the “initial marriage commitment” as challenging as that may be.

The Word of God holds the initial marriage covenant exclusively binding and honorable. Any subsequent marriage vow while either spouse is living is considered by our Lord as the sin of lust and adultery and must be repented of if we wish to seek God’s forgiveness.

Therefore, repentance and forgiveness by both spouses, with the desire to reunite and honor their initial God-blessed marriage covenant, is not a desire of the flesh but is the work of the Holy Spirit deep within the heart of the sinner. When there is a godly desire to repent and reconcile a broken relationship, we should fall on our knees in support and sincere gratitude to our Heavenly Father.

Jesus has offered to come between and restore struggling relationships that through humility and repentance seek forgiveness, thus returning to full service for their Lord resulting in eternal joy. He says: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them –Matthew 18:20. And Paul says, But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you –Romans 8:11.

Derfor er de ikke lenger to, men ett kjøtt … –Matteus 19:6.

Ekteskapet ble innstiftet av Gud helt fra tidens begynnelse. Gud tilbød også å velsigne ekteskapet (1. Mosebok 1:28) mellom mannen og kvinnen som inngikk det, dersom de ønsket å bevare dets skjønnhet og hellighet. Siden den gang har Satan på alle mulige måter forsøkt å forderve og ødelegge det hellige ekteskapet. Allerede i 1. Mosebok 4:19 brukte menneskene polygami for å forvrenge Guds plan for ekteskapet. I 3. Mosebok, kapittel 21 og 22, ble det innført en ordning, kalt skilsmisse, for juridisk å oppløse «den første kjærligheten». Dette omfattet også muligheten til å gifte seg på nytt. Da skilsmisse først ble innført som praksis, var det mennesket, ikke Gud, som tok initiativ til den, og hensikten var å oppløse det som fram til da ble forstått som en livslang forpliktelse.

I denne artikkelen vil vi se på en rekke spørsmål:

  • Hva lærer Bibelen om ekteskapet? Har det første ekteskapet en særskilt plass hos Gud?
  • Hva lærer Bibelen om skilsmisse? Anerkjenner Gud skilsmisse som en avslutning på det opprinnelige ekteskapsløftet mens en av ektefellene fortsatt lever?
  • Hva lærer Bibelen om gjenforening av et separert eller skilt første ekteskap?

Hensikten med denne studien er å være omfattende, samtidig som Skriften får tolke seg selv, og derfor holde kommentarer på et minimum. Målet med denne teksten er å oppmuntre til flittig bønn i søken etter Guds vilje gjennom studium av hans Ord. Skribenten har ønsket å overveie alle relevante skriftsteder og sammenhengen de ble skrevet i, under bønn.

Hva lærer Bibelen om Guds syn på det første ekteskapet?

Minst fem ganger i Det gamle testamentet beskriver Herren det første ekteskapet som eksklusivt og livslangt. Jesus og apostlene i Det nye testamentet støttet det samme synet.

  1. La din kilde være velsignet, og gled deg over din ungdoms hustru –Ordspråkene 5:18. Legg merke til hvor mye vekt som legges på din ungdoms hustru.

  2. For Herren har kalt deg som en forlatt og åndelig bedrøvet kvinne, som en ungdomshustru som ble forkastet, sier din Gud –Jesaja 54:6. At hun var ungdomshustru og senere ble forkastet, forsterket sorgen hos denne forlatte kvinnen.

  3. Likevel sier dere: «Hvorfor?» Fordi Herren har vært vitne mellom deg og din ungdoms hustru, som du har vært troløs mot, enda hun er din ledsager og din pakts hustru. Var det ikke én som gjorde henne? Likevel hadde han en rest av Ånden. Og hvorfor én? For at han skulle søke en guddommelig ætt. Ta derfor vare på deres ånd, og vær ikke troløse mot din ungdoms hustru. For Herren, Israels Gud, sier at han hater å skille seg fra sin hustru. Den ene dekker vold med kappen sin, sier hærskarenes Herre. Ta derfor vare på deres ånd, så dere ikke handler troløst. –Malaki 2:14–16. Og hvorfor ble de gjort til ett, slik at de tilhører hverandre alene? For å oppdra en gudfryktig ætt for Herren. Selv om Gud hater at man skiller seg fra sin hustru, forsøker menn fortsatt å dekke over dette med en kappe av sivilrettslig, juridisk aksept som kalles «skilsmisse».

  4. Matteus 19:3–12: Vers 4: «I begynnelsen …» Da fariseerne spurte Jesus om dette, fører han dem tilbake til sin Fars opprinnelige hensikt og irettesetter dem: Han svarte: «Har dere ikke lest at Skaperen fra begynnelsen skapte dem til mann og kvinne?» –Matteus 19:4. Deretter minner han dem om Skriftens lære om at … en mann skal forlate sin far og sin mor og holde fast ved sin hustru, og de to skal være ett kjøtt. Så er de ikke lenger to, men ett kjøtt. Det som Gud har sammenføyd, skal mennesket ikke skille. –Matteus 19:5–6. Ikke likestill menneskelig myndighet (den sivile domstolen) med Guds myndighet når det gjelder å avgjøre hva som er fakta angående ekteskap, skilsmisse og gjengifte. Vi må huske at det er Gud som har sammenføyd hvert ekteskap i himmelen og skrevet det inn i Livets bok.

  5. En gift kvinne er ved lov bundet til mannen sin så lenge han lever. Men dersom mannen dør, er hun løst fra loven som bandt henne til mannen. Hvis hun altså, mens mannen lever, blir en annen manns hustru, skal hun kalles en ekteskapsbryter. Men dersom mannen dør, er hun fri fra loven, så hun ikke er en ekteskapsbryter selv om hun blir en annen manns hustru. –Romerne 7:2–3. Også her vises det tilbake til begynnelsen for å etablere et grunnlag for sannheten.

Bare en av ektefellenes død vil avslutte den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten i de himmelske registrene. Og når dette livet er over, er det bare de himmelske registrene som vil ha betydning – i all evighet.

Det finnes flere unntak fra det bibelske idealet:

  • Hold ikke tilbake fra hverandre, bortsett fra når dere etter gjensidig samtykke gjør det for en tid, for å kunne vie dere til bønn og faste. Kom så sammen igjen, for at ikke Satan skal friste dere fordi dere mangler selvbeherskelse. –1. Korinter 7:5. Å avstå fra ekteskapelig samliv en tid, med frivillig samtykke fra både mann og kone, kan altså i noen tilfeller føre til Guds velsignelse når det er behov for å søke Guds gunst eller veiledning i en svært viktig sak. Dette bør imidlertid bare gjøres dersom begge ektefellene har en klar forståelse av og forpliktelse til når og hvordan de skal komme sammen igjen, så Satan ikke frister dem. Dette unntaket har tre tydelige vilkår … 1) med samtykke, 2) for en tid, og 3) med det formål å vie dere til bønn og faste.

  • Til de gifte gir jeg dette påbudet – ikke jeg, men Herren: En kone må ikke skille seg fra mannen sin. Men dersom hun likevel skiller seg, skal hun forbli ugift eller forsone seg med mannen sin. Og en mann må ikke skille seg fra sin kone. –1. Korinter 7:10–11. Dette er skriftstedet som fritar den uskyldige ektefellen for bibelsk skyld når den andre ektefellen er den som valgte å gå sin vei. Likevel gjelder fortsatt læren om at de ikke skal gifte seg med en annen «så lenge den opprinnelige ektefellen er i live».

Hva lærer Bibelen om Guds syn på skilsmisse?

Det er sagt: «Den som skiller seg fra sin kone, skal gi henne skilsmissebrev.» Men jeg sier dere: Den som skiller seg fra sin kone av noen annen grunn enn hor, gjør at hun blir utsatt for ekteskapsbrudd. Og den som gifter seg med en fraskilt kvinne, bryter ekteskapet. –Matteus 5:31–32. Da Jesus underviste folket i Bergprekenen, var et av de mange temaene han stadig vendte tilbake til, Guds opprinnelige plan for ekteskapet.

«Av noen annen grunn enn hor» Hor er enhver form for umoral før ekteskapet. Kristne i vår tid strever noen ganger med denne tanken, siden skikkene i den gamle jødiske kulturen for lengst er glemt. I jødisk kultur ble forlovelsestiden regnet som nesten like bindende som selve ekteskapsinngåelsen, så mye at det krevdes en «skilsmisse» for å avslutte en forlovelse. Med dette som utgangspunkt handler hor her om umoral i trolovelses- eller forlovelsestiden. Hvis utroskap ble oppdaget, måtte man skrive skilsmissebrev for å bryte trolovelsen, forlovelsen eller ekteskapsløftet. Jesus kritiserte ikke dette særlige aspektet ved skilsmisse. Selv om de ikke hadde lov til å ha ekteskapelig samliv i forlovelsestiden, ble de likevel omtalt som mann og kone. Grunnen til at dette kalles hor og ikke ekteskapsbrudd, er til sist at de to ennå ikke var blitt gift i forlovelsestiden, og at forholdet deres ennå ikke var fullbyrdet fysisk. Derfor ville ethvert forhold til en annen rett før det tidspunktet da Gud regner dem som gift, være hor, mens et tilsvarende forhold rett etter at de regnes som gift, ville være ekteskapsbrudd.

Vi har et utmerket bibelsk eksempel på denne typen situasjon i de følgende versene om Josef og Maria: Med Jesu Kristi fødsel gikk det slik til: Maria, hans mor, var trolovet med Josef. Før de var kommet sammen, viste det seg at hun var gravid ved Den hellige ånd. Josef, mannen hennes, var rettskaffen og ville ikke føre skam over henne offentlig. Derfor bestemte han seg for å skille seg fra henne i all stillhet. –Matteus 1:18–19.

Bibelsk sett kan skilsmisse altså skille det første ekteskapet i henhold til sivil lov, men kan ikke avslutte et første ekteskap for Gud. En fraskilt person forblir den første ektefellens ledsager (så lenge den andre ektefellen lever), også når vedkommende gifter seg på nytt, enten skilsmissen er juridisk gyldig eller ikke, og dermed blir begge parter skyldige i ekteskapsbrudd ifølge Bibelen. Men når skilsmisse får anerkjennes som gyldig i å bryte eller annullere den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten, har vi dermed fjernet den konkrete grunnen til at Gud kaller senere ekteskap ekteskapsbrudd.

I Matteus 19:3–10 lærer Jesus den samme leksen som i Matteus 5:31–32. Men Matteus 19:3–10 begynte med at fariseerne forsøkte å fange Jesus med et spørsmål: De spør ham: «Hvorfor ga da Moses påbud om å gi kvinnen skilsmissebrev og skille seg fra henne?» –Matteus 19:7. Jesus svarer videre: … Moses tillot dere å skille dere fra konene deres fordi dere har harde hjerter. Men fra begynnelsen var det ikke slik. –Matteus 19:8.

Også i Markus står det skrevet: Men fra skapelsens begynnelse skapte Gud dem til mann og kvinne. Derfor skal mannen forlate sin far og sin mor og holde fast ved sin kone, og de to skal være ett kjøtt. Så er de ikke lenger to, men ett kjøtt. Det som Gud har sammenføyd, skal mennesket ikke skille. –Markus 10:6–9.

Skilsmisse, med alle sine regler, er altså menneskets forsøk på å bruke sivil lov til å avslutte det som fra begynnelsen ble forstått å vare til en av ektefellene døde.

Hva lærer Bibelen om gjenforening av et separert eller skilt første ekteskap?

Han sa til dem: «Moses tillot dere å skille dere fra konene deres fordi dere har harde hjerter. Men fra begynnelsen var det ikke slik.» –Matteus 19:8. Her lærer Jesus om sin Fars opprinnelige hensikt. I loven lærte Moses at … Når en mann har tatt en kvinne til ekte og giftet seg med henne, og det så skjer at hun ikke finner nåde for hans øyne fordi han har funnet noe usømmelig hos henne, skal han skrive et skilsmissebrev, gi det til henne og sende henne ut av huset sitt. Når hun har forlatt huset hans, kan hun bli en annen manns kone. Dersom den siste mannen hennes får avsky for henne, skriver et skilsmissebrev, gir det til henne og sender henne ut av huset sitt, eller dersom den siste mannen, som tok henne til kone, dør, da kan ikke hennes første mann, som sendte henne bort, ta henne tilbake som kone … –5. Mosebok 24:1–4.

Dette er Moses’ lære om tillatelse til skilsmisse og vilkårene for den, som Jesus forklarte var fordi de hadde harde hjerter. Jesus presiserte dette ytterligere da han sa: Men fra begynnelsen var det ikke slik. –Matteus 19:8.

Det kan hende Jeremia også viser til Moses’ ord i 5. Mosebok 24:1–4 når han sier: Det sies: «Hvis en mann skiller seg fra sin kone, og hun går fra ham og blir en annen manns, kan han da vende tilbake til henne? Ville ikke landet bli grovt vanhelliget?» Men du har drevet hor med mange elskere, og likevel skal du vende tilbake til meg, sier Herren. –Jeremia 3:1. Resten av Jeremia kapittel 3 handler om at Gud tar dem tilbake hvis de vender om. Gud ber dem (vers 13) «erkjenne din skyld» (omvende seg), og kaller dem gjentatte ganger til å vende tilbake (vers 14–).

Gud inviterte Israel tilbake til fellesskap med ham på grunnlag av at hun erkjente sin synd og endret sin ferd, uten å ta hensyn til den forskriften Moses ga i 5. Mosebok 24:1–4, fordi «fra begynnelsen var det ikke slik».

I Jeremia 3:8 hadde Herren skilt seg fra henne (Israel) og gitt henne skilsmissebrev. Men i vers 1 og 12 inviterer han henne til å vende tilbake, og i vers 14 tilbyr han vilkårene for forsoning. Hos Malaki står det skrevet: Juda har vært troløs, og det er gjort avskyelige ting i Israel og Jerusalem. Juda har vanhelliget Herrens helligdom, som han elsker, og giftet seg med en datter av en fremmed gud. –Malaki 2:11.

At Gud skilte seg fra Israel, og at Israel deretter giftet seg på nytt med en fremmed gud, hindret på ingen måte at de vendte tilbake til sitt første ekteskap. Herren inviterte dem i stedet tilbake dersom de ville omvende seg, Jeremia 3:13–14. På den tiden 5. Mosebok kapittel 24 ble skrevet, og gjennom det meste av Det gamle testamentet, var skilsmisse blitt vanlig og akseptert, og menneskene forsøkte å sette noen regler for den, «men fra begynnelsen var det ikke slik».

I Hoseas bok har vi et bibelsk eksempel på gjenforening av et separert eller skilt første ekteskap: … Herren sa til Hosea: «Gå og ta deg en horkvinne og horbarn! For landet driver stadig hor ved å vende seg bort fra Herren.» –Hosea 1:2 (se også Hosea 2:5).

En tid etter at Hosea gifter seg med henne, vender hun tilbake til livet som «horkvinne» (Hosea 3:3) og går etter andre «elskere» (2:7). Når hun omtaler Hosea som «min første mann» (2:7), er det et tegn på at hun sannsynligvis giftet seg på nytt etter å ha forlatt Hosea. (2:14) Ved at Hosea tålmodig «lokket henne og talte vennlig til henne» (2:19–20), trolovet Hosea henne på nytt, og Gomer ser ut til å ha svart (2:20) «i trofasthet» og kommet til å «kjenne Herren». (3:3) Til slutt ble Hosea og Gomer gjenforent, forpliktet til å være trofaste mot hverandre.

Gjenopprettelse av den opprinnelige, Gud-innstiftede forpliktelsen er målet, forsoning er prosessen, og et angrende hjerte for Herren, som søker hans barmhjertighet og tilgivelse, er middelet (se Hosea 3:5).

Johannes 4:1–42 er et skriftsted som noen vil tolke som en innvending mot gjenforening av et første ekteskap etter separasjon eller skilsmisse, på grunn av Jesu svar til kvinnen. Etter at hun sa «Jeg har ingen mann.» Jesus sa til henne: «Du har rett når du sier: ‘Jeg har ingen mann.’ For du har hatt fem menn, og den du nå har, er ikke din mann. Der sa du sant.» –Johannes 4:17–18.

Noen vil tolke Jesus slik at han sier: «Du har rett, kvinne: Ingen av de fem tidligere mennene dine som du har skilt deg fra eller sendt bort (inkludert den første), er mannen din, og heller ikke den du har nå.» Noen bibelkommentatorer og andre omtaler denne kvinnen som en som har vært skilt fem ganger og nå lever sammen med en mann uten å være gift. Jeg finner imidlertid ingen belegg i denne beretningen for at kvinnen levde et ugudelig liv.

Hensikten med denne beretningen er at Jesus skal åpenbare seg for kvinnen og mange andre i Sykar som «Messias» med «levende vann». Jesus sier ingenting for å bebreide eller korrigere henne, noe han vanligvis ville gjort når han møtte synd. Alle de fem mennene kan ha vært døde, og den hun nå traff, kan bare ha vært en venn, kanskje med ekteskap i tankene. Vi vet det ikke, for teksten sier det ikke. Men hun ser ut til å ha vært en kvinne med respekt og innflytelse i byen, noe som ville vært lite sannsynlig dersom hun hadde hatt et vedvarende rykte for umoral. Jesus ville sikkert ha sagt noe for å gjøre henne oppmerksom på synden hennes da han tilbød henne sitt levende vann. Derfor stemmer det ikke med resten av Skriften å bruke denne beretningen til å si at alle de fem mennene fortsatt er ekteskapsbrytende ektemenn som Gud regner som hennes ektemenn. Det støtter heller ikke sammenhengen i utsagnet: den du nå har, er ikke din mann. Å hevde at denne fortellingen viser et umoralsk liv uten kjent bibelsk belegg, er nær ved å «legge til» eller «trekke fra» Skriften. (Se Åpenbaringen 22:18)

Avslutningsvis … I vår verden i dag, og gjennom historien, har menneskene forsøkt å likestille ekteskap som inngås etter skilsmisse med den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten. Dette har forvirret og svekket den vekten og hensikten Gud har lagt på den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten. Guds Ord lærer at Herren alltid har respektert omvendelse når en opprinnelig pakt som Gud har velsignet, blir gjenopprettet. For at Herren skal velsigne og fremme forsoning i et vanskelig forhold, krever han en sønderbrutt, angrende og ydmyk ånd, som underordner seg.

Sammenhengen i 1. Korinter 7:10–16 er at en troende er i et paktsforhold med en ektefelle som ikke tror. I vers 15 er den troende ektefellen som blir igjen, ikke forpliktet til å fornekte sin trosvandring for å fortsette ekteskapet. Vedkommende står heller ikke fritt til å gifte seg på nytt (vers 11) dersom den ikke-troende ektefellen går. Hvis vers 15 handler om ekteskapspakten, ville vers 39 være i strid med vers 15 og Guds vilje slik den framgår av resten av Skriften (se Matteus 19:5 og 1. Korinter 7:10). Å bo hver for seg begrenser innflytelsen på familien og er et negativt vitnesbyrd for lokalsamfunnet. Derfor vil den troende ektefellen alltid ha langt større innvirkning for Herren ved å holde fast ved «den opprinnelige ekteskapsforpliktelsen», hvor krevende det enn måtte være.

Guds Ord holder den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten utelukkende bindende og ærverdig. Ethvert senere ekteskapsløfte mens en av ektefellene fortsatt lever, regnes av vår Herre som lystens synd og ekteskapsbrudd, og må det omvendes fra dersom vi ønsker å søke Guds tilgivelse.

Omvendelse og tilgivelse hos begge ektefellene, sammen med ønsket om å bli gjenforent og ære den opprinnelige ekteskapspakten Gud har velsignet, er derfor ikke et ønske som springer ut av kjødet, men Den hellige ånds verk dypt i synderens hjerte. Når det finnes et gudfryktig ønske om å omvende seg og forsone et ødelagt forhold, bør vi falle på kne i støtte og oppriktig takknemlighet til vår himmelske Far.

Jesus har tilbudt seg å komme imellom og gjenopprette forhold som strever, når de søker tilgivelse gjennom ydmykhet og omvendelse, slik at de igjen kan tjene sin Herre fullt ut og få evig glede. Han sier: For der to eller tre er samlet i mitt navn, der er jeg midt iblant dem. –Matteus 18:20. Og Paulus sier: Hvis hans Ånd som reiste Jesus opp fra de døde, bor i dere, skal han som reiste Kristus opp fra de døde, også gjøre deres dødelige kropper levende ved sin Ånd som bor i dere. –Romerne 8:11.

Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh… –Matthew 19:6.

The marriage relationship was authored by God in the very beginning of time. God also offered to bless the marriage (Genesis 1:28) of the man and woman entering into it, if they desired to maintain its beauty and holiness. Since then, Satan has attempted, in every way possible, to corrupt and destroy the existence of Holy Matrimony. As early as Genesis 4:19, mankind was using polygamy to corrupt God's design of marriage. In Leviticus chapters 21 and 22, a plan, called a divorce, was put in place to legally dissolve the “first love”. This also included the option to remarry. When it was first developed as a practice, the call for divorce was initiated by man, not God, and was for the purpose of dissolving what was understood up until that time to be a lifelong commitment.

In this article we want to look at a number of points:

  • What does the Bible teach about marriage? Does the first marriage carry any special position with God?
  • What does the Bible teach about divorce? Does God recognize divorce as terminating the original marriage vow while either spouse is still living?
  • What does the Bible teach about the reuniting of a separated or divorced first marriage?

It is the desire of this study to be comprehensive, while allowing the scriptures to be their own interpreter, thus keeping commentary to a minimum. The purpose of this writing is to encourage diligence with prayer in seeking the will of God through a study of His Word. The desire of the writer has been to prayerfully consider all relevant scriptures and the context for which they were written.

What does the Bible teach about God's view of the first marriage?

At least five times in the Old Testament, the first marriage is described by the Lord as exclusive and lifelong. This same view was supported by Jesus and the apostles in the New Testament.

  1. Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth –Proverbs 5:18. Note the attention given to the wife of thy youth.

  2. For the LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God –Isaiah 54:6. Being a wife of one’s youth and then later refused, intensified the grieving of this forsaken woman.

  3. Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant. And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously. –Malachi 2:14-16. And why are they made one, exclusive to each other? To raise up a godly seed unto the Lord. Even though God hates putting away, men still try to cover it with a garment of civil, legal acceptance called "divorce".

  4. Matthew 19:3-12: V.4 In the beginning… Jesus, when asked by the Pharisees about this issue, takes them back to original intent of His Father when He chides them… And he answered and said unto them, Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female –Matthew 19:4. He then goes on to remind them of the Scriptures teaching that …a man [shall] leave [his] father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder –Matthew 19:5-6. Don't equate man’s authority (the civil court) with God’s authority when it comes to deciding what the facts are concerning marriage, divorce, and remarriage. We need to remember that it is God who has joined each marriage together in Heaven and has recorded them in the Book of Life.

  5. For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband. So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man –Romans 7:2-3. Again, this is pointing back to the beginning in order to establish a basis of Truth.

Only the death of either spouse will terminate the initial marriage covenant in the heavenly records. And once this life is over, only the heavenly records will matter—for all of eternity.

There are several exceptions to the Biblical ideal:

  • Defraud [deprive, keep back] ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency [lack of self-restraint] –1 Corinthians 7:5. So, restraining the marriage relationship for a time with voluntary consent from both husband and wife when there is a need for seeking God’s favor or guidance on a matter of great importance, may in some circumstances find God’s blessing. However, this should only be engaged in with a clear understanding and commitment by both spouses involved, about when and how to come together again, lest Satan tempt you. This exception has three clear qualifiers… 1) with consent, 2) for a time, & 3) for the purpose of giving yourselves to prayer and fasting.

  • And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband: But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife –1 Corinthians 7:10-11. This is the Scriptural passage that frees the innocent spouse from biblical guilt when the other spouse is the one who chose to part ways. However, the teaching still remains that they shall not marry another “so long as the original partner remains alive”.

What does the Bible teach about God's view of divorce?

It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery –Matthew 5:31-32. As Jesus taught the people in His Sermon on the Mount, one of the many things that He kept focusing on was this issue of God’s original plan for marriage.

“Saving for the cause of fornication” Fornication is any type of immorality prior to marriage. Modern-day Christianity, at times, struggles with this idea since the customs of the ancient Jewish culture have long since been forgotten. In Jewish culture, the betrothal period was considered almost as binding as the marriage ceremony itself, so much so that to end a betrothal required a “divorce”. With this as a foundational understanding, fornication here is speaking of immorality during the espousal or betrothal period. If any unfaithfulness was discovered, a writing of divorcement was required to break the betrothal, espousal, or engagement. This specific aspect of divorce was not criticized by Jesus. Even though they were not permitted to engage in the physical relationship of marriage during the betrothal period, they were still referred to as husband and wife. Finally, the reason this is referred to as fornication instead of adultery is because that during the betrothal period the marriage of the two has not yet taken place, nor has their relationship been consummated physically. Thus, just prior to the point in time when they are considered by God as being married, any outside relationship would be fornication, while just after they are considered married, any similar relationship would be adultery.

We have an excellent biblical example of this type of situation with Joseph & Mary in the following verses: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily –Matthew 1:18, 19.

So, biblically speaking, divorce can put asunder the first marriage according to civil law but cannot terminate a first marriage before God. A divorced person remains the companion of their first marriage (as long as the other spouse is alive) even when remarrying, whether they are legally divorced or not, thus resulting in biblical adultery for both parties. However, when divorce is allowed to be recognized as being legitimate in breaking or annulling the initial marriage covenant, we have thereby removed the specific reason by which God calls subsequent marriages adultery.

In Matthew 19:3-10, Jesus is teaching the same lesson as in Matthew 5:31-32. However, Matthew 19:3-10 was initiated from an attempt by the Pharisees to trap Jesus with a question: They say unto him, Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away? –Matthew 19:7. Jesus then responds further and says, …Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8.

Also, in Mark it is written, But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female. For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and cleave to his wife; And they twain shall be one flesh: so then they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder –Mark 10:6-9.

Thus, divorce, with all its regulations, is man's attempt to use civil law to terminate that which from the beginning was understood to be until the death of either spouse.

What does the Bible teach about the reuniting of a separated or a divorced first marriage?

He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8. Here Jesus is teaching the initial mind of His Father. In the law, Moses taught that… When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house. And when she is departed out of his house, she may go and be another man's wife. And if the latter husband hate her, and write her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand, and sendeth her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, which took her to be his wife; Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife… –Deuteronomy 24:1-4.

This is Moses' teaching regarding permission and qualifications for divorce which Jesus explained was because of the hardness of their hearts. Jesus further clarified this by saying, but from the beginning it was not so –Matthew 19:8.

Perhaps Jeremiah also is referring to Moses' writing in Deuteronomy 24:1-4 when he says, They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man's, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted? but thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the LORD –Jeremiah 3:1. The remainder of Jeremiah chapter 3 speaks of God receiving them back if they repent. God pleads for them to (v.13) "acknowledge thine iniquity" (repent), and repeatedly calls for their return (v.14-)

God invited Israel back into fellowship with Him on the basis of acknowledging her sin and changing her ways, giving no heed to the instruction that Moses gave in Deuteronomy 24:1-4, because "from the beginning it was not so."

In Jeremiah 3:8, the Lord had put her (Israel) away and given her a bill of divorcement. But in verses 1 and 12, He invites her to return and in verse 14 He offers the terms of reconciliation. In Malachi it is written, Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god –Malachi 2:11.

God's divorcing of Israel and Israel's subsequent remarriage to a strange god in no way interfered with them returning to their first marriage. Instead, the Lord invited them back if they would repent, Jeremiah 3:13-14. By the time of Deuteronomy chapter 24 and through most of the Old Testament, divorce was the accepted normal, with mankind attempting to put some regulations on it, "but from the beginning it was not so."

In the book of Hosea, we have a biblical example of the reuniting of a separated or divorced first marriage: … And the LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD –Hosea 1:2 (see also Hosea 2:5).

Sometime after Hosea marries her, she resorts to the life of a "harlot'' (Hosea 3:3) and goes after other "lovers" (2:7). When she refers to Hosea as "my first husband" (2:7), it is evidence that she likely remarried after deserting Hosea. (2:14) By Hosea patiently "alluring her and speaking comfortably to her" (2:19-20), Hosea betrothed her again and Gomer apparently responded (2:20) "in faithfulness” and came to "know the Lord." (3:3) Eventually, Hosea and Gomer both reunited with a commitment of faithfulness to each other.

Restoration to the initial God-ordained commitment is the goal, reconciliation is the process, and a repentant heart before the Lord for His mercy and forgiveness is the means (see Hosea 3:5).

John 4:1-42 is a scripture that some would interpret as objecting to the reuniting of a first marriage after a separation or divorce, because of Jesus' reply to the woman. After she said …I have no husband. Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly –John 4:17-18.

Some would interpret Jesus to be saying, "You are right woman, none of your five former husbands of which you have divorced or put away (including your first one) are your husband, and neither is the one you have now. Some commentators and others refer to this woman as a five-time divorcee and currently living with a man in an unmarried state. However, I find no evidence in this account that this woman was living an unholy life.

Jesus' purpose of this account is to reveal Himself as the "Messias" with "Living Water" to this woman and many more in Sychar. Jesus says nothing to fault or correct her, which He typically would when meeting with sin. All five husbands could have been passed away and the one she was now seeing, just a friend, perhaps anticipating marriage. Also, we don't know since it doesn't say, but she seemed to be a woman of respect and influence in the city, which would have been unlikely with an ongoing reputation of immorality. Jesus would surely have said something to inform her of her sin, when making available His Living Water. So, to use this account and say that all five husbands are adulterous and still classified as God-recorded husbands does not agree with the rest of Scripture. Nor does it support the context of the statement: he whom thou now hast is not thy husband. To claim that this story is a display of an immoral lifestyle with no known biblical evidence is close to “adding to” or “taking away” from the Scriptures. (See Revelation 22:18)

In conclusion… In our world today and in history past, mankind has attempted to equate subsequent marriages following a divorce, to the level of the initial marriage covenant. This has confused the emphasis and intent God has put on the initial marriage covenant. God's Word teaches that the Lord has always respected repentance in the restoration of any initial God-blessed covenant. For the Lord to bless and prosper the reconciling of any struggling relationship, He requires a broken, contrite spirit of humility and repentance with submission.

The context of 1 Corinthians 7:10-16 is that of a believer being in a covenant relationship with a spouse who is an unbeliever. In verse 15, the remaining believing spouse is not under obligation to denounce their walk of faith to continue a marriage relationship, neither are they free to remarry (verse 11) in the event of the unbelieving spouse leaving. If verse 15 is speaking of the marriage covenant, then verse 39 would contradict verse 15 and the will of God according to the rest of Scripture, (see Matthew 19:5 and 1 Corinthians 7:10). Living separately limits influence to the family and is a negative witness to the community, thus the believing spouse will always have a much greater impact for the Lord by staying true to the “initial marriage commitment” as challenging as that may be.

The Word of God holds the initial marriage covenant exclusively binding and honorable. Any subsequent marriage vow while either spouse is living is considered by our Lord as the sin of lust and adultery and must be repented of if we wish to seek God’s forgiveness.

Therefore, repentance and forgiveness by both spouses, with the desire to reunite and honor their initial God-blessed marriage covenant, is not a desire of the flesh but is the work of the Holy Spirit deep within the heart of the sinner. When there is a godly desire to repent and reconcile a broken relationship, we should fall on our knees in support and sincere gratitude to our Heavenly Father.

Jesus has offered to come between and restore struggling relationships that through humility and repentance seek forgiveness, thus returning to full service for their Lord resulting in eternal joy. He says: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them –Matthew 18:20. And Paul says, But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you –Romans 8:11.

So sind sie nun nicht mehr zwei, sondern ein Fleisch … –Matthäus 19,6.

Die Ehe wurde von Gott ganz am Anfang der Zeit eingesetzt. Gott bot auch an, die Ehe (1. Mose 1,28) des Mannes und der Frau, die sie eingingen, zu segnen, wenn sie ihre Schönheit und Heiligkeit bewahren wollten. Seitdem hat Satan auf jede erdenkliche Weise versucht, die Existenz der heiligen Ehe zu verderben und zu zerstören. Schon in 1. Mose 4,19 bediente sich die Menschheit der Polygamie, um Gottes Plan für die Ehe zu verderben. In den Kapiteln 21 und 22 des 3. Buches Mose wurde ein Verfahren eingeführt, das Scheidung genannt wurde und die rechtliche Auflösung der „ersten Liebe“ ermöglichte. Dazu gehörte auch die Möglichkeit einer Wiederheirat. Als diese Praxis erstmals eingeführt wurde, ging die Forderung nach Scheidung von Menschen aus, nicht von Gott, und diente dazu, das aufzulösen, was bis dahin als lebenslange Verpflichtung verstanden worden war.

In diesem Artikel wollen wir mehrere Punkte betrachten:

  • Was lehrt die Bibel über die Ehe? Hat die erste Ehe bei Gott eine besondere Stellung?
  • Was lehrt die Bibel über die Scheidung? Erkennt Gott eine Scheidung als Beendigung des ursprünglichen Ehegelübdes an, solange einer der Ehepartner noch lebt?
  • Was lehrt die Bibel über die Wiedervereinigung einer getrennten oder geschiedenen ersten Ehe?

Diese Studie möchte umfassend sein und zugleich der Schrift gestatten, sich selbst auszulegen, sodass der Kommentar auf ein Minimum beschränkt bleibt. Dieser Text soll dazu ermutigen, im Gebet eifrig Gottes Willen durch das Studium seines Wortes zu suchen. Der Verfasser hat sich bemüht, alle relevanten Schriftstellen und den Zusammenhang, in dem sie geschrieben wurden, unter Gebet zu bedenken.

Was lehrt die Bibel über Gottes Sicht auf die erste Ehe?

Mindestens fünfmal wird die erste Ehe im Alten Testament vom Herrn als exklusiv und lebenslang beschrieben. Jesus und die Apostel vertraten im Neuen Testament dieselbe Sichtweise.

  1. Dein Born sei gesegnet, und freue dich der Frau deiner Jugend –Sprüche 5,18. Beachten Sie, dass der Frau deiner Jugend besondere Aufmerksamkeit gilt.

  2. Der HERR hat dich berufen wie eine verlassene und im Geist betrübte Frau, wie eine Frau der Jugend, die verschmäht worden ist, spricht dein Gott –Jesaja 54,6. Dass sie die Frau seiner Jugend gewesen und später verschmäht worden war, verstärkte den Kummer dieser verlassenen Frau.

  3. Und ihr fragt: Warum? Weil der HERR Zeuge war zwischen dir und der Frau deiner Jugend, an der du treulos gehandelt hast, obwohl sie deine Gefährtin und die Frau deines Bundes ist. Hat er sie nicht zu einem gemacht? Und doch hatte er einen Rest des Geistes. Und warum einen? Damit er eine gottesfürchtige Nachkommenschaft suche. So nehmt euch in Acht um eures Geistes willen und handle keiner treulos an der Frau seiner Jugend. Denn der HERR, der Gott Israels, spricht, dass er das Entlassen hasst; denn einer bedeckt sein Gewand mit Gewalttat, spricht der HERR der Heerscharen. So nehmt euch in Acht um eures Geistes willen und handelt nicht treulos. –Maleachi 2,14-16. Und warum wurden sie zu einem gemacht, einander vorbehalten? Um dem Herrn eine gottesfürchtige Nachkommenschaft aufzuziehen. Obwohl Gott das Entlassen hasst, versuchen Menschen weiterhin, es mit dem Mantel einer staatlichen, rechtlichen Anerkennung zu bedecken, die „Scheidung“ genannt wird.

  4. Matthäus 19,3-12: Vers 4: Am Anfang … Als die Pharisäer Jesus zu dieser Frage befragten, führte er sie auf den ursprünglichen Willen seines Vaters zurück und hielt ihnen vor: Und er antwortete und sprach zu ihnen: Habt ihr nicht gelesen, dass der, welcher sie am Anfang geschaffen hat, sie als Mann und Frau geschaffen hat? –Matthäus 19,4. Dann erinnert er sie an die Lehre der Schrift: … Ein Mann wird Vater und Mutter verlassen und seiner Frau anhangen, und die zwei werden ein Fleisch sein. So sind sie nun nicht mehr zwei, sondern ein Fleisch. Was nun Gott zusammengefügt hat, das soll der Mensch nicht scheiden. –Matthäus 19,5-6. Setzen Sie die Autorität des Menschen (des Zivilgerichts) nicht mit Gottes Autorität gleich, wenn es darum geht, die Tatsachen bezüglich Ehe, Scheidung und Wiederheirat festzustellen. Wir müssen bedenken, dass Gott jede Ehe im Himmel zusammengefügt und sie im Buch des Lebens aufgezeichnet hat.

  5. Eine Frau ist durch das Gesetz an ihren Mann gebunden, solange er lebt; ist aber der Mann gestorben, so ist sie vom Gesetz des Mannes frei. Wenn sie also, solange der Mann lebt, einem anderen Mann angehört, wird sie Ehebrecherin genannt; ist aber der Mann gestorben, so ist sie von diesem Gesetz frei, sodass sie keine Ehebrecherin ist, wenn sie einem anderen Mann angehört. –Römer 7,2-3. Auch hier wird auf den Anfang zurückverwiesen, um eine Grundlage der Wahrheit festzulegen.

Nur der Tod eines der Ehepartner beendet den ursprünglichen Ehebund in den himmlischen Aufzeichnungen. Und wenn dieses Leben vorüber ist, werden nur die himmlischen Aufzeichnungen zählen – in alle Ewigkeit.

Es gibt mehrere Ausnahmen vom biblischen Ideal:

  • Beraubt einander nicht, außer mit gegenseitiger Zustimmung für eine Zeit, damit ihr euch dem Fasten und dem Gebet widmen könnt; und kommt dann wieder zusammen, damit Satan euch nicht wegen eurer Unenthaltsamkeit [mangelnden Selbstbeherrschung] versucht. –1. Korinther 7,5. Die eheliche Beziehung für eine Zeit auszusetzen, mit freiwilliger Zustimmung von Mann und Frau, wenn es darum geht, Gottes Gunst oder Führung in einer sehr wichtigen Angelegenheit zu suchen, kann also unter Umständen Gottes Segen finden. Dies sollte jedoch nur geschehen, wenn beide Ehepartner klar verstehen und sich dazu verpflichten, wann und wie sie wieder zusammenkommen, damit Satan euch nicht versucht. Diese Ausnahme hat drei eindeutige Voraussetzungen … 1) mit Zustimmung, 2) für eine Zeit und 3) zu dem Zweck, sich dem Gebet und Fasten zu widmen.

  • Den Verheirateten aber gebiete nicht ich, sondern der Herr: Die Frau soll sich nicht von ihrem Mann trennen. Wenn sie sich aber trennt, soll sie unverheiratet bleiben oder sich mit ihrem Mann versöhnen; und der Mann soll seine Frau nicht entlassen. –1. Korinther 7,10-11. Diese Schriftstelle bewahrt den unschuldigen Ehepartner vor biblischer Schuld, wenn der andere Ehepartner die Trennung gewählt hat. Dennoch bleibt die Lehre bestehen, dass sie keinen anderen heiraten sollen, „solange der ursprüngliche Partner lebt“.

Was lehrt die Bibel über Gottes Sicht auf die Scheidung?

Es ist gesagt worden: Wer seine Frau entlässt, der gebe ihr einen Scheidebrief. Ich aber sage euch: Wer seine Frau entlässt, außer wegen Unzucht, der veranlasst sie, Ehebruch zu begehen; und wer eine Entlassene heiratet, begeht Ehebruch. –Matthäus 5,31-32. Als Jesus die Menschen in seiner Bergpredigt lehrte, richtete er seinen Blick immer wieder auf diesen Punkt: Gottes ursprünglicher Plan für die Ehe.

„Außer wegen Unzucht“ Unzucht ist jede Art von Unmoral vor der Ehe. Das heutige Christentum tut sich mit dieser Vorstellung manchmal schwer, weil die Bräuche der alten jüdischen Kultur längst in Vergessenheit geraten sind. In der jüdischen Kultur galt die Verlobungszeit als beinahe ebenso verbindlich wie die Trauung, sodass eine Verlobung nur durch eine „Scheidung“ beendet werden konnte. Vor diesem Hintergrund bezieht sich Unzucht hier auf Unmoral während der Verlobungszeit. Wurde Untreue entdeckt, war ein Scheidebrief erforderlich, um die Verlobung zu lösen. Jesus kritisierte diesen besonderen Aspekt der Scheidung nicht. Obwohl es ihnen während der Verlobungszeit nicht erlaubt war, die eheliche körperliche Beziehung einzugehen, wurden sie dennoch als Mann und Frau bezeichnet. Schließlich wird dies als Unzucht und nicht als Ehebruch bezeichnet, weil die Ehe der beiden während der Verlobungszeit noch nicht geschlossen und ihre Beziehung körperlich noch nicht vollzogen war. Daher wäre jede außereheliche Beziehung unmittelbar vor dem Zeitpunkt, an dem Gott sie als verheiratet betrachtet, Unzucht, während eine ähnliche Beziehung unmittelbar nachdem sie als verheiratet gelten, Ehebruch wäre.

Ein ausgezeichnetes biblisches Beispiel für eine solche Situation finden wir in den folgenden Versen über Josef und Maria: Die Geburt Jesu Christi geschah aber so: Als seine Mutter Maria dem Josef verlobt war, noch bevor sie zusammenkamen, wurde sie schwanger gefunden vom Heiligen Geist. Josef aber, ihr Mann, der gerecht war und sie nicht öffentlich bloßstellen wollte, gedachte, sie heimlich zu entlassen. –Matthäus 1,18-19.

Biblisch gesehen kann eine Scheidung die erste Ehe nach staatlichem Recht scheiden, aber eine erste Ehe vor Gott nicht beenden. Ein geschiedener Mensch bleibt mit seinem ersten Ehepartner verbunden (solange der andere Ehepartner lebt), auch wenn er wieder heiratet, gleichgültig, ob die Scheidung rechtmäßig ist oder nicht; dadurch begehen beide Parteien nach der Bibel Ehebruch. Wenn man jedoch eine Scheidung als rechtmäßige Auflösung oder Aufhebung des ursprünglichen Ehebundes anerkennt, beseitigt man damit den besonderen Grund, aus dem Gott spätere Ehen Ehebruch nennt.

In Matthäus 19,3-10 lehrt Jesus dieselbe Lektion wie in Matthäus 5,31-32. Matthäus 19,3-10 geht jedoch auf den Versuch der Pharisäer zurück, Jesus mit einer Frage in eine Falle zu locken: Sie sagen zu ihm: Warum hat Mose dann geboten, einen Scheidebrief zu geben und sie zu entlassen? –Matthäus 19,7. Jesus antwortet darauf weiter: … Mose hat euch wegen der Härte eurer Herzen erlaubt, eure Frauen zu entlassen; von Anfang an aber ist es nicht so gewesen. –Matthäus 19,8.

Auch bei Markus steht geschrieben: Von Anfang der Schöpfung an aber hat Gott sie als Mann und Frau geschaffen. Darum wird ein Mann seinen Vater und seine Mutter verlassen und seiner Frau anhangen, und die zwei werden ein Fleisch sein; so sind sie nicht mehr zwei, sondern ein Fleisch. Was nun Gott zusammengefügt hat, das soll der Mensch nicht scheiden. –Markus 10,6-9.

So ist die Scheidung mit all ihren Vorschriften der Versuch des Menschen, mithilfe des Zivilrechts etwas zu beenden, das von Anfang an als bis zum Tod eines der Ehepartner bestehend verstanden wurde.

Was lehrt die Bibel über die Wiedervereinigung einer getrennten oder geschiedenen ersten Ehe?

Er sagte zu ihnen: Mose hat euch wegen der Härte eurer Herzen erlaubt, eure Frauen zu entlassen; von Anfang an aber ist es nicht so gewesen –Matthäus 19,8. Hier lehrt Jesus die ursprüngliche Absicht seines Vaters. Im Gesetz lehrte Mose: Wenn ein Mann eine Frau genommen und sie geheiratet hat und es geschieht, dass sie keine Gunst in seinen Augen findet, weil er etwas Anstößiges an ihr gefunden hat, so soll er ihr einen Scheidebrief schreiben, ihn ihr in die Hand geben und sie aus seinem Haus entlassen. Wenn sie dann aus seinem Haus gegangen ist, kann sie die Frau eines anderen Mannes werden. Wenn aber der spätere Mann sie hasst, ihr einen Scheidebrief schreibt, ihn ihr in die Hand gibt und sie aus seinem Haus entlässt, oder wenn der spätere Mann stirbt, der sie zu seiner Frau genommen hat, dann darf ihr früherer Mann, der sie entlassen hat, sie nicht wieder zur Frau nehmen … –5. Mose 24,1-4.

Das ist Moses Lehre über die Erlaubnis zur Scheidung und die dafür geltenden Voraussetzungen, die Jesus mit den Worten erklärte: wegen der Härte ihrer Herzen. Jesus verdeutlichte dies noch, indem er sagte: von Anfang an aber ist es nicht so gewesen –Matthäus 19,8.

Vielleicht bezieht sich auch Jeremia auf Moses Schriften in 5. Mose 24,1-4, wenn er sagt: Es heißt: Wenn ein Mann seine Frau entlässt und sie von ihm weggeht und die Frau eines anderen wird, darf er wieder zu ihr zurückkehren? Würde jenes Land dadurch nicht völlig entweiht? Du aber hast mit vielen Liebhabern Unzucht getrieben und solltest dennoch zu mir zurückkehren?, spricht der HERR. –Jeremia 3,1. Im übrigen Teil von Jeremia 3 geht es darum, dass Gott sie wieder aufnimmt, wenn sie umkehren. Gott fleht sie an, (Vers 13) „deine Schuld anzuerkennen“ (umzukehren), und ruft sie wiederholt zur Rückkehr auf (Vers 14 ff.).

Gott lud Israel ein, wieder in Gemeinschaft mit ihm zu treten, wenn sie ihre Sünde anerkannte und ihren Weg änderte; dabei beachtete er die Anweisung nicht, die Mose in 5. Mose 24,1-4 gegeben hatte, denn „von Anfang an war es nicht so“.

In Jeremia 3,8 hatte der Herr sie (Israel) entlassen und ihr einen Scheidebrief gegeben. Doch in den Versen 1 und 12 lädt er sie zur Rückkehr ein, und in Vers 14 nennt er die Bedingungen für die Versöhnung. Bei Maleachi steht geschrieben: Juda hat treulos gehandelt, und in Israel und in Jerusalem ist ein Gräuel begangen worden; denn Juda hat das Heiligtum des HERRN entweiht, das er liebte, und die Tochter eines fremden Gottes geheiratet. –Maleachi 2,11.

Dass Gott sich von Israel scheiden ließ und Israel anschließend einen fremden Gott heiratete, hinderte sie keineswegs daran, zu ihrer ersten Ehe zurückzukehren. Vielmehr lud der Herr sie ein, zurückzukehren, wenn sie umkehren würden, Jeremia 3,13-14. Zur Zeit von 5. Mose 24 und während des größten Teils des Alten Testaments war die Scheidung allgemein üblich; die Menschen versuchten, ihr gewisse Regeln aufzuerlegen, „aber von Anfang an war es nicht so“.

Im Buch Hosea finden wir ein biblisches Beispiel für die Wiedervereinigung einer getrennten oder geschiedenen ersten Ehe: … Und der HERR sprach zu Hosea: Geh hin, nimm dir eine Frau der Hurerei und Kinder der Hurerei; denn das Land treibt große Hurerei, indem es sich vom HERRN abwendet. –Hosea 1,2 (siehe auch Hosea 2,5).

Einige Zeit nach Hoseas Heirat mit ihr verfällt sie dem Leben einer „Hure“ (Hosea 3,3) und läuft anderen „Liebhabern“ nach (2,7). Als sie Hosea als „meinen ersten Mann“ bezeichnet (2,7), ist das ein Hinweis darauf, dass sie Hosea wahrscheinlich verließ und danach wieder heiratete. (2,14) Indem Hosea sie geduldig „lockte und freundlich zu ihr sprach“ (2,19-20), verlobte Hosea sich erneut mit ihr, und Gomer antwortete offenbar (2,20) „in Treue“ und kam dazu, „den HERRN zu erkennen“. (3,3) Schließlich kamen Hosea und Gomer wieder zusammen und verpflichteten sich zu gegenseitiger Treue.

Die Wiederherstellung der ursprünglichen, von Gott eingesetzten Verpflichtung ist das Ziel, Versöhnung ist der Prozess, und ein bußfertiges Herz vor dem Herrn, um seine Barmherzigkeit und Vergebung zu erlangen, ist der Weg dahin (siehe Hosea 3,5).

Johannes 4,1-42 ist eine Schriftstelle, die manche als Einwand gegen die Wiedervereinigung einer ersten Ehe nach Trennung oder Scheidung verstehen, und zwar wegen Jesu Antwort an die Frau. Nachdem sie gesagt hatte: … Ich habe keinen Mann. Jesus sprach zu ihr: Du hast recht gesagt: Ich habe keinen Mann. Denn fünf Männer hast du gehabt, und der, den du jetzt hast, ist nicht dein Mann; darin hast du die Wahrheit gesagt. –Johannes 4,17-18.

Manche würden Jesus so verstehen, als sage er: „Du hast recht, Frau: Keiner deiner fünf früheren Männer, von denen du dich scheiden ließest oder die du entlassen hast (einschließlich deines ersten), ist dein Mann, und auch der, den du jetzt hast, ist es nicht.“ Manche Kommentatoren und andere bezeichnen diese Frau als fünfmal geschiedene Frau, die derzeit unverheiratet mit einem Mann zusammenlebt. Ich finde in diesem Bericht jedoch keinen Beleg dafür, dass diese Frau ein sündiges Leben führte.

Jesus wollte sich in dieser Begegnung der Frau und vielen anderen in Sychar als der „Messias“ mit „lebendigem Wasser“ offenbaren. Jesus sagt nichts, um sie zurechtzuweisen oder zu korrigieren, wie er es gewöhnlich tat, wenn er mit Sünde konfrontiert wurde. Alle fünf Männer könnten gestorben sein, und der, den sie nun traf, könnte lediglich ein Freund gewesen sein, vielleicht in der Hoffnung auf eine spätere Ehe. Wir wissen es nicht, denn der Text sagt es nicht. Doch sie scheint eine angesehene und einflussreiche Frau in der Stadt gewesen zu sein, was bei einem anhaltenden Ruf der Unmoral unwahrscheinlich wäre. Jesus hätte gewiss etwas gesagt, um sie auf ihre Sünde hinzuweisen, als er ihr sein lebendiges Wasser anbot. Daher stimmt es nicht mit dem übrigen Teil der Schrift überein, diesen Bericht heranzuziehen und zu behaupten, alle fünf Männer seien ehebrecherisch und weiterhin als von Gott verzeichnete Ehemänner zu betrachten. Auch der Zusammenhang der Aussage der, den du jetzt hast, ist nicht dein Mann stützt diese Deutung nicht. Zu behaupten, diese Geschichte schildere einen unmoralischen Lebenswandel, obwohl es dafür keine bekannten biblischen Belege gibt, kommt dem „Hinzufügen“ oder „Wegnehmen“ von der Schrift nahe. (Siehe Offenbarung 22,18.)

Abschließend … In unserer heutigen Welt und in der Vergangenheit hat die Menschheit versucht, späteren Ehen nach einer Scheidung denselben Rang wie dem ursprünglichen Ehebund zu geben. Dadurch wurden die Bedeutung und die Absicht verwischt, die Gott dem ursprünglichen Ehebund beigelegt hat. Gottes Wort lehrt, dass der Herr stets die Umkehr bei der Wiederherstellung jedes ursprünglichen, von Gott gesegneten Bundes anerkannt hat. Damit der Herr die Versöhnung einer schwierigen Beziehung segnet und gedeihen lässt, verlangt er einen zerbrochenen, reumütigen Geist der Demut und Umkehr sowie Unterordnung.

Der Zusammenhang von 1. Korinther 7,10-16 handelt von einem Gläubigen, der in einem Ehebund mit einem ungläubigen Ehepartner lebt. In Vers 15 ist der gläubige Ehepartner, der bleibt, nicht verpflichtet, seinem Glaubensweg abzusagen, um die eheliche Beziehung fortzusetzen; ebenso wenig ist er frei, im Fall des Weggangs des ungläubigen Ehepartners wieder zu heiraten (Vers 11). Wenn Vers 15 vom Ehebund spricht, widerspräche er Vers 39 und dem Willen Gottes, wie er sich aus dem übrigen Teil der Schrift ergibt (siehe Matthäus 19,5 und 1. Korinther 7,10). Getrennt zu leben schränkt den Einfluss auf die Familie ein und ist für die Gemeinschaft ein negatives Zeugnis. Daher wird der gläubige Ehepartner immer einen viel größeren Einfluss für den Herrn haben, wenn er der „ursprünglichen ehelichen Verpflichtung“ treu bleibt, so herausfordernd das auch sein mag.

Das Wort Gottes hält den ursprünglichen Ehebund ausschließlich bindend und ehrwürdig. Jedes spätere Ehegelübde, solange einer der Ehepartner lebt, gilt unserem Herrn als Sünde der Begierde und des Ehebruchs und muss bereut werden, wenn wir Gottes Vergebung suchen wollen.

Darum ist die Umkehr und Vergebung beider Ehepartner, verbunden mit dem Wunsch, sich wiederzuvereinigen und ihren ursprünglichen, von Gott gesegneten Ehebund zu ehren, kein Wunsch des Fleisches, sondern das Wirken des Heiligen Geistes tief im Herzen des Sünders. Wenn der gottesfürchtige Wunsch besteht, umzukehren und eine zerbrochene Beziehung zu versöhnen, sollten wir auf die Knie fallen, um unseren himmlischen Vater zu unterstützen und ihm aufrichtig zu danken.

Jesus hat angeboten, in schwierige Beziehungen hineinzutreten und sie wiederherzustellen, wenn Menschen in Demut und Umkehr um Vergebung bitten; so können sie ihrem Herrn wieder uneingeschränkt dienen und ewige Freude erfahren. Er sagt: Denn wo zwei oder drei in meinem Namen versammelt sind, da bin ich mitten unter ihnen. –Matthäus 18,20. Und Paulus sagt: Wenn aber der Geist dessen, der Jesus von den Toten auferweckt hat, in euch wohnt, so wird der, der Christus von den Toten auferweckt hat, auch eure sterblichen Leiber lebendig machen durch seinen Geist, der in euch wohnt. –Römer 8,11.
